family: REST integration guide for asynchronous financial record exports
task: Finalize this draft for backend integrators implementing Ledgerlake CSV exports, including polling, pagination, and retry handling.
source_facts: Ledgerlake is a synthetic ledger service. Authenticated clients with the exports:write scope create exports with POST /v2/exports and a JSON body containing account_id, the ledger account whose records are exported. A successful creation response is HTTP 202 with export_id, the stable identifier of the export job, and snapshot_at, the fixed data cutoff timestamp chosen when the job is accepted. 202 means accepted for processing, not that a file is ready. Every result page belongs to that snapshot; subsequent ledger writes do not enter it. Send an Idempotency-Key header on creation. Reusing that key with the same body within 24 hours of the first accepted request returns the same job. Reusing it with a different body within that window returns 409. GET /v2/exports/EXPORT_ID returns 202 while processing and 303 with a Location header pointing to the first result page when ready. Poll no faster than once every 2 seconds. On any 429 response, Retry-After gives the required wait in seconds before the next request. A result-page GET returns CSV and a next_after response header. Each page has at most 500 data rows; the CSV header row does not count toward that limit. The after query parameter carries an opaque token from next_after and must not be constructed by clients. The final page has the literal next_after value null. Each issued page token expires 30 minutes after the response that issued it. An expired token is recovered by requesting GET /v2/exports/EXPORT_ID to obtain a fresh first-page Location and restarting traversal; the snapshot does not change. Result files expire 24 hours after the job becomes ready, independently of token expiration. After file expiration, retrieval returns 410 and the client must create a new export with a new Idempotency-Key. The new job has a newly chosen snapshot_at. An account with no matching records is the rare empty-result case: its first page returns 200, contains only the CSV header row, and has next_after: null. DELETE /v2/exports/EXPORT_ID removes export artifacts but never deletes source ledger records. A useful integration log records export_id, snapshot_at, and the last successfully processed page token; tokens remain opaque even when logged. A new traversal after token expiry can revisit rows, so the consumer must account for revisited rows in its own processing.

# Export account records with Ledgerlake

Use this guide when an integration needs a bounded CSV view of one ledger account. Your authenticated client needs the exports:write scope. Keep job creation, readiness polling, and result-page consumption as separate steps so that the application can show progress while Ledgerlake prepares the export.

## Request a job

Send `POST /v2/exports` with a JSON body containing account_id, the account whose ledger records you want. Include an `Idempotency-Key` header. If you repeat the same key and body within 24 hours of the first accepted request, Ledgerlake returns the same job. A different body with that key in the same window returns 409. This lets a client recover from an uncertain creation response without deliberately creating another export.

A successful request returns 202. The export_id is the stable identifier of the export job, not an identifier for a ledger account. The snapshot_at timestamp is the fixed data cutoff selected when the job is accepted. Every page belongs to that snapshot, so ledger writes accepted afterward do not appear partway through the download.

## Wait for readiness

Request `GET /v2/exports/EXPORT_ID` to check the job. A 202 response means processing is still underway; it does not mean a CSV file is ready. A 303 response supplies the first result-page URL in the Location header.

Poll no faster than once every 2 seconds. On a 429 response, wait for the number of seconds specified by Retry-After before sending the next request. Apply that response-specific wait to whichever export request received the 429.

## Walk the result pages

Fetch the Location URL to receive CSV. A page contains at most 500 data rows, excluding the CSV header row. The next_after response header provides the token for the next page. Supply it unchanged as the after query parameter; it is opaque and is not a row number that the client can increment. The literal value `null` in next_after marks the final page.

There is a useful empty-account exception to recognize in fixtures and production handling. When the account has no matching records, the first page still returns 200 and contains the CSV header row. Its next_after value is null. Treat that as a completed empty export rather than a missing file or a polling response.

## Recover an interrupted traversal

A page token lasts 30 minutes from the response that issued it. When that token expires, request the job again to obtain a fresh first-page Location and restart traversal. This recovery uses the existing snapshot. Since it can revisit rows, the consumer needs to account for those rows in its own processing.

The file lifetime is a different clock: result files expire 24 hours after the job becomes ready. Once retrieval returns 410 because that lifetime has ended, create a new export with a new Idempotency-Key. The replacement job gets a newly selected snapshot_at rather than extending the previous snapshot.

## Scheduling note

Poll no faster than once every 2 seconds. On a 429 response, wait for the number of seconds specified by Retry-After before sending the next request. Apply that response-specific wait to whichever export request received the 429.

## Record what was delivered

Log export_id, snapshot_at, and the last page token your consumer processed successfully. Recording a token does not make its contents an interface: continue treating it as an opaque value. These log fields distinguish the job, its data cutoff, and the position reached by this particular consumer.

The timestamp named snapshot_at describes the data boundary fixed at job acceptance. Pages do not drift forward as you read them, and writes made after that boundary stay outside the export. This remains true throughout the multi-page result.

## Remove finished artifacts

Use `DELETE /v2/exports/EXPORT_ID` when you want to remove the export artifacts. That operation never deletes the underlying ledger records. Artifact cleanup therefore serves a different purpose from choosing a new snapshot or consuming the next result page.

requirements.description: account_id identifies the ledger account whose records the job exports.
snapshot_at is the job-acceptance data cutoff shared by all result pages, excluding later ledger writes.
HTTP 202 means the export is accepted or processing rather than ready to download.
A ready job returns 303 with its first result-page URL in Location.
Normal polling is limited to once every 2 seconds or slower.
Retry-After on a 429 specifies the wait before the next request in seconds.
The page limit is 500 data rows excluding the CSV header row.
after carries the opaque next_after token unchanged rather than a client-constructed row position.
The literal next_after value null means that the page is final.
A page token expires 30 minutes after the response that issued it.
Token-expiration recovery restarts traversal from a fresh first-page Location for the same snapshot.
Result files expire 24 hours after the job becomes ready.
A 410 caused by file expiration requires a new export with a new Idempotency-Key.
The empty-result exception is a successful 200 first page containing only the CSV header and next_after: null.
Reusing an Idempotency-Key with the same body within 24 hours of first acceptance returns the same job.
Reusing an Idempotency-Key with a different body within its 24-hour window returns 409.
Deleting an export removes artifacts without deleting source ledger records.
